ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: 1 of 1 paper appeared to involve live data collection and lacked an ethics approval statement.

table.text: Participants were 1,393 adults from the Collaborative Study on the Genetics of Alcohol Lifespan assessment (Mage= 52.0, 59.7% female).

Participants were categorized into four mutually exclusive groups: no lifetime AUD or CUD (i.e., AUD-/CUD-), AUD without CUD (i.e., AUD+/CUD-), CUD without AUD (i.e., AUD-/CUD+), and comorbid AUD + CUD (i.e., AUD+/CUD+).

With respect to AUD and CUD diagnostic group membership, 33.5% (N= 467) of participants were in the AUD-/CUD-group, 32.0% (N= 446) were in the AUD+/CUD-group, 28.4% (N= 396) were in the comorbid AUD+/CUD+ group, and 6% (N= 84) were in the AUD-/CUD+ group.
A related consequence is that relatively few participants had CUD without AUD (n= 84; 6.0% of the analytic sample).

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = c("p > 0.05", "p-values < 0.05"), 
    Text = c("51.72 years, p = 0.035), but no significant differences were observed for sex distribution, AUD diagnosis, CUD diagnosis, MDD diagnosis, past-year alcohol use, past-year nicotine use, or past-year cannabis use (all p > 0.05).", 
    "The bolded coefficients (95% CI) are statistically significant with adjusted p-values < 0.05 (after multi-test correction by FDR)."
    )), row.names = c(NA, -2L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"
))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association. :::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = "p > 0.05", Sentence = "51.72 years, p = 0.035), but no significant differences were observed for sex distribution, AUD diagnosis, CUD diagnosis, MDD diagnosis, past-year alcohol use, past-year nicotine use, or past-year cannabis use (all p > 0.05)."), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame")) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see [Improving Your Statistical Inferences](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/01-pvalue.html#sec-misconception1). :::

text.text: Background.
Alcohol use disorder (AUD) and cannabis use disorder (CUD) are often comorbid.
Concurrent or simultaneous use of alcohol and cannabis is associated with poorer mental health outcomes in cross-sectional studies.
Here, we examined whether lifetime history of comorbid AUD and CUD is associated with emotional well-being, above and beyond current substance use and lifetime major depression.
Methods.
Participants were 1,393 adults from the Collaborative Study on the Genetics of Alcohol Lifespan assessment (Mage= 52.0, 59.7% female).

Emotional well-being was assessed across six domains from the NIH Toolbox Emotion Battery: loneliness, perceived stress, negative affect, social satisfaction, psychological well-being, and self-efficacy.

Associations between lifetime diagnostic group (comorbid AUD + CUD, AUD without CUD, CUD without AUD, or neither disorder) and emotional well-being outcomes were assessed using multivariate linear regression.
Covariates included age, sex, and past-year nicotine, cannabis, and alcohol use.
Sensitivity analyses adjusted for lifetime major depressive disorder.
Results.

Individuals with comorbid lifetime AUD + CUD reported higher loneliness, perceived stress, and negative affect, and lower social satisfaction, psychological well-being, and selfefficacy compared to other groups.

Individuals with lifetime AUD without CUD or CUD without AUD generally resembled those with neither disorder across several emotional well-being domains, though those in the AUD without CUD group reported greater negative affect and lower social satisfaction and psychological well-being than the group with neither disorder.

A lifetime history of comorbid AUD and CUD is associated with diminished emotional well-being, underscoring the need for additional psychosocial supports to address these challenges in this population.

Alcohol use disorder (AUD) and cannabis use disorder (CUD) are the two most common substance use disorders in the United States and are associated with substantial public health costs (Blanco et al., 2026; Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration, 2019).

text.text: Despite these high rates of comorbidity, little is known about the emotional well-being of those with lifetime comorbid AUD and CUD compared to those affected by just one of these disorders.

Much of what is known about the associations between emotional well-being and alcohol and cannabis use comes from studies of co-use or co-occurring disorders (Hetelekides et al., 2025; Howe et al., 2025; Metrik et al., 2018).

text.text: For example, both concurrent alcohol and cannabis use (i.e., use of both within a given time period) and simultaneous use (i.e., use of both on the same occasion) have been linked to greater substance-related harms and poorer mental health outcomes, including elevated depression, anxiety, and stress symptoms, relative to use of either substance alone (Briere et al., 2011; Linden-Carmichael et al., 2021).

text.text: Additionally, individuals with co-occurring AUD and CUD (i.e., both disorders being clinically active within the same time frame) have greater odds of interpersonal, financial, legal, and health-related problems than individuals with neither disorder or individuals with one disorder but not the other (Gutkind et al., 2021).

text.text: Although prior studies provide important insight into the relationship between combined alcohol and cannabis involvement and emotional functioning, several research gaps remain.
First, existing studies have largely relied on young adult or college student samples and cross-sectional designs (Hetelekides et al., 2025).

text.text: This has left unanswered questions about the longerterm correlates of alcohol and cannabis involvement, which are often dynamic across the life course (Linden-Carmichael et al., 2021).

text.text: Second, it remains unclear whether these findings extend to individuals with a lifetime history of comorbid AUD and CUD, even after adjusting for current levels of use.

Prospective longitudinal data underscore that there is a high degree of heterogeneity in the individual sequencing of AUD and CUD or other drug use disorder diagnoses (Kosty et al., 2017; Reilly et al., 2017), and that these disorders are associated with enduring neurobiological changes related to reward processing and negative affect (Hand et al., 2024; Zehra et al., 2018).

text.text: The heterogeneity in these patterns highlights the need for a more nuanced understanding of the long-term correlates of diagnostic comorbidity, as many individuals with diagnostic comorbidity are overlooked in cross-sectional studies of co-occurring disorders.
Third, research on substance involvement and emotional functioning has often relied on limited indicators of mental health, such as depression and anxiety (McHugh and Weiss, 2019).

text.text: There is growing recognition of the importance of measuring emotional well-being multidimensionally to include a broader range of negative affective experiences such as perceived stress and loneliness (McHugh and Weiss, 2019).

text.text: Moreover, as much of the prior work in this area has emphasized indicators of negative emotionality, far less attention has been paid to positive emotional dimensions such as social satisfaction, psychological well-being, and selfefficacy (Schotanus-Dijkstra et al., 2017).

text.text: To address these gaps, in the present study we examined whether emotional well-being, as indexed by both negative (loneliness, perceived stress, negative affect) and positive (social satisfaction, psychological well-being, and self-efficacy) dimensions, differed among adults with lifetime comorbid AUD and CUD compared to those with AUD without CUD, CUD without AUD, or no lifetime history of either disorder, and whether any differences were observed after statistically adjusting for current substance use.

In view of the prior literature (Gutkind et al., 2021), we hypothesized that individuals with lifetime comorbid AUD and CUD would report diminished emotional well-being across domains relative to those with a single disorder or those with neither.

text.text: We further expected that individuals with AUD without CUD or CUD without AUD would report lower emotional well-being compared to people with neither AUD nor CUD, although these associations would be smaller in magnitude than those observed for the comorbid group.

We also conducted a sensitivity analysis adjusting for lifetime major depressive disorder (MDD), which frequently co-occurs with both AUD and CUD (Pacek et al., 2013) and is itself associated with poorer emotional well-being (Proudman et al., 2021), to evaluate whether associations between diagnostic group and emotional well-being were robust to this potential confound.

text.formatted: <head n="2." >Methods</head>

text.text: Data came from the Collaborative Study on the Genetics of Alcoholism (COGA), a multisite, family-based longitudinal study designed to examine genetic and environmental influences on AUD and related psychopathology (Dick et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Data came from the Collaborative Study on the Genetics of Alcoholism (COGA), a multisite, family-based longitudinal study designed to examine genetic and environmental influences on AUD and related psychopathology <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Dick et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: The present analyses used data from the 2019-2024 COGA Lifespan assessment, which was a follow-up that targeted adult participants from earlier phases of COGA to better characterize the course and consequences of AUD across adulthood.

The analytic sample examined here included the 1,390 adults who completed the NIH Emotion Toolbox (Salsman et al., 2013) as part of that assessment, plus 3 young adult COGA participants for whom the NIH Emotion Toolbox data were collected as part of a spin-off study.

text.text: Participants ranged from 29 to 87 years old (M= 52.0 years, SD= 14.6), and 59.7% were female.

The primary predictor was lifetime diagnostic group, defined based on lifetime AUD and CUD diagnoses assessed using the Semi-Structured Assessment for the Genetics of Alcoholism (Bucholz et al., 1994) according to DSM-5 criteria (American Psychiatric Association, 2013).

text.text: Participants were categorized into four mutually exclusive groups: no lifetime AUD or CUD (i.e., AUD-/CUD-), AUD without CUD (i.e., AUD+/CUD-), CUD without AUD (i.e., AUD-/CUD+), and comorbid AUD + CUD (i.e., AUD+/CUD+).
Emotional well-being was assessed using age-adjusted T-scores from the NIH Toolbox Emotion Battery (Version 2), which was administered via an iPad (Toolbox Assessments Inc., 2015).
The NIH Toolbox Emotion Battery was developed for large-scale epidemiologic and clinical research as a brief, comprehensive assessment of emotional well-being across adulthood (Salsman et al., 2013).
text.formatted: The NIH Toolbox Emotion Battery was developed for large-scale epidemiologic and clinical research as a brief, comprehensive assessment of emotional well-being across adulthood <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Salsman et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: The measures include: loneliness (perceived social isolation and lack of companionship), perceived stress (the extent to which individuals feel overwhelmed or unable to cope with life demands), negative affect (frequency of negative emotional experiences such as sadness or anger), social satisfaction (perceived quality and fulfillment of social relationships), psychological well-being (overall sense of purpose, meaning and life satisfaction) and self-efficacy (confidence in one's ability to manage challenges and achieve goals).
Our adjusted models included demographic, substance use, and clinical covariates.
Demographic covariates included age and sex.
Past-year substance use covariates were included to distinguish between the effects of current substance use and lifetime history of AUD and CUD.

They included a binary measure of nicotine use (inclusive of cigarettes, cigars, pipe tobacco, hookah, chewing tobacco, or e-cigarettes), the number of cannabis use occasions, and alcohol use, measured as days in the past year.
Nicotine use was controlled for because it commonly co-occurs with alcohol and cannabis use, and is itself associated with lower emotional well-being (Leventhal and Zvolensky, 2015).
text.formatted: Nicotine use was controlled for because it commonly co-occurs with alcohol and cannabis use, and is itself associated with lower emotional well-being <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Leventhal and Zvolensky, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: In sensitivity analyses, we also adjusted for lifetime MDD, given elevated rates of depression among individuals with comorbid AUD and CUD and the overlap between depressive symptoms and the emotional well-being outcomes examined here (McHugh and Weiss, 2019; Sorkhou et al., 2024).
text.formatted: In sensitivity analyses, we also adjusted for lifetime MDD, given elevated rates of depression among individuals with comorbid AUD and CUD and the overlap between depressive symptoms and the emotional well-being outcomes examined here <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(McHugh and Weiss, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Sorkhou et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: We used multivariate regression models to jointly estimate associations and account for the covariance among the six emotional well-being outcomes.
Analyses were conducted using the lavaan package in R (Rosseel, 2012).
text.formatted: Analyses were conducted using the lavaan package in R <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Rosseel, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: To account for the non-independence of observations, a family-level clustering variable was specified in lavaan, which implements sandwich (Huber-White) robust standard errors that adjust for within-family correlation.
To address the study's research questions, multivariate models were estimated using two different reference groups.
First, models were estimated with the AUD+/CUD+ group as the reference, allowing direct comparisons between the lifetime comorbid group and the singledisorder groups.
Second, models were estimated with no lifetime AUD or CUD (i.e., AUD-/CUD-) as the reference, allowing for comparisons between this group and the single-disorder groups.

To control the false discovery rate associated with multiple comparisons, p-values from the regression analyses were adjusted within each research question using the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure (Benjamini and Hochberg, 1995).
text.formatted: To control the false discovery rate associated with multiple comparisons, p-values from the regression analyses were adjusted within each research question using the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Benjamini and Hochberg, 1995)</ref>.

text.text: All models adjusted for demographic and past-year substance use covariates.

To evaluate whether associations between diagnostic group and emotional well-being were attributable to comorbid depression, we conducted sensitivity analyses in which all multivariate models were re-estimated with lifetime MDD included as an additional covariate.
>Results
text.formatted: <head n="3." >Results</head>

text.text: Of the 3,784 participants in the Lifespan sample, 1,390 completed the NIH Emotion Toolbox and were included in the analytic sample.

Toolbox data were only available on a subset of the Lifespan sample because completion of the Toolbox required an in-person visit, and the data collection timeframe overlapped with the COVID public health emergency.

Other components of the Lifespan assessment protocol could be completed telephonically, but restrictions on in-person assessments at COGA study sites resulted in a reduced sample for Toolbox measures.

To evaluate potential selection bias and sample representativeness, demographic and substance use characteristics were compared between the full Lifespan sample and the analytic sample using independent-samples t-tests for normally distributed continuous variables, Wilcoxon rank-sum tests for non-normally distributed variables, and chi-square tests for categorical variables.
The analytic sample was slightly older on average than the overall sample (mean age = 52.72 vs.

51.72 years, p = 0.035), but no significant differences were observed for sex distribution, AUD diagnosis, CUD diagnosis, MDD diagnosis, past-year alcohol use, past-year nicotine use, or past-year cannabis use (all p > 0.05).

text.text: Overall, 59.2% met criteria for lifetime AUD and 34.5% met criteria for lifetime CUD.

With respect to AUD and CUD diagnostic group membership, 33.5% (N= 467) of participants were in the AUD-/CUD-group, 32.0% (N= 446) were in the AUD+/CUD-group, 28.4% (N= 396) were in the comorbid AUD+/CUD+ group, and 6% (N= 84) were in the AUD-/CUD+ group.
With respect to past-year substance use, 34.5% of participants reported nicotine use, an average of 78 drinking days, and an average of 50 cannabis use occasions.
Correlations among emotional well-being outcomes are depicted in Supplemental Figure 1.

text.text: There were moderate to strong associations across domains, with several correlations exceeding r = .50, particularly between negative affect and perceived stress and between psychological well-being and social satisfaction.

The results from the adjusted multivariate analyses comparing emotional well-being in the comorbid AUD+/CUD+ group with the other diagnostic groups are depicted in Figure 1 and full results are summarized in Supplemental Table 1.

text.text: The comorbid AUD+/CUD+ group reported higher loneliness, perceived stress, and negative affect and lower social satisfaction, psychological well-being, and self-efficacy than both the AUD+/CUD-group, the AUD-/CUD+ group, and the group with neither disorder (AUD-/CUD-).
The one exception to this was that loneliness and social satisfaction in the AUD-/CUD+ group did not differ significantly from the comorbid group.
To evaluate whether the observed effects were attributable to comorbid major depression diagnoses, we re-estimated the model after adjusting for lifetime MDD (Supplemental Table 2).

text.text: The pattern was largely unchanged, with two exceptions.

Self-efficacy in the AUD-/CUD-and AUD+/CUD-groups no longer differed significantly from the comorbid group after MDD adjustment, and social satisfaction in the AUD-/CUD+ group, which did not differ from the comorbid group in the primary model, was significantly higher than in the comorbid group after MDD adjustment.

To further characterize emotional well-being differences across diagnostic groups, we examined whether emotional well-being outcomes differed between the group of people with neither AUD nor CUD (i.e., AUD-/CUD-) and those with one of those disorders (i.e., AUD+/CUD-or AUD-/CUD+).
The results from these models are depicted in Figure 2 and the full results are summarized in Supplemental Table 3.
text.formatted: The results from these models are depicted in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2</ref> and the full results are summarized in Supplemental Table <ref type="table">3</ref>.

text.text: Individuals in the AUD-/CUD+ group did not differ significantly from those in the AUD-/CUD-group on any emotional well-being outcome after covariate adjustment, in contrast to our hypotheses.
However, individuals in the AUD+/CUD-group reported significantly greater negative affect, lower social satisfaction, and lower psychological well-being relative to the AUD-/CUD-group.
There were no significant differences observed between the AUD+/CUD-and AUD-/CUD-groups on loneliness, perceived stress, or self-efficacy.

In the sensitivity analysis adjusting for lifetime MDD (Supplemental Table 4), the AUD-/CUD+ group still did not differ from the AUD-/CUD-group on any outcome, and the AUD+/CUD-group continued to report greater negative affect and lower social satisfaction, but the difference in psychological well-being was no longer significant.

>Discussion
text.formatted: <head n="4." >Discussion</head>

text.text: The present study examined the associations between lifetime comorbid AUD and CUD diagnostic groups and six domains of emotional well-being in adulthood.

A consistent pattern emerged, whereby people with lifetime comorbid AUD and CUD reported higher loneliness, higher perceived stress, higher negative affect, lower social satisfaction, lower psychological well-being, and lower self-efficacy compared to people with neither disorder and those with one disorder but not the other.
The two exceptions to this general trend were that loneliness and social satisfaction did not differ between people in the comorbid group and people with lifetime CUD but not AUD.
There was partial evidence for our hypothesis that emotional well-being would differ between people with a lifetime AUD or CUD diagnosis compared to the group with neither disorder.
People with AUD but not CUD had higher negative affect, lower social satisfaction, and lower psychological well-being compared to people with neither disorder.
These associations remained evident even after accounting for current nicotine, alcohol, and cannabis use.

Furthermore, this overall pattern was largely robust to adjustment for MDD, though selfefficacy differences between the comorbid group and the AUD-/CUD-and AUD+/CUD-groups were attenuated after MDD adjustment.

Individuals with comorbid AUD+/CUD+ exhibited the poorest emotional well-being across domains, extending prior findings that combined alcohol and cannabis involvement and past-year concurrent diagnoses are associated with greater psychiatric burden, poorer functioning, and elevated depression, anxiety, stress and emotional dysregulation relative to single-substance use (Duncan et al., 2015; Gutkind et al., 2021; Hetelekides et al., 2025; McHugh and Weiss, 2019; Metrik et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Individuals with comorbid AUD+/CUD+ exhibited the poorest emotional well-being across domains, extending prior findings that combined alcohol and cannabis involvement and past-year concurrent diagnoses are associated with greater psychiatric burden, poorer functioning, and elevated depression, anxiety, stress and emotional dysregulation relative to single-substance use <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Duncan et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Gutkind et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Hetelekides et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">McHugh and Weiss, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Metrik et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Notably, poorer emotional well-being among people with comorbid AUD and CUD was not limited to elevated negative emotional states such as perceived stress or negative affect.
People with comorbid AUD and CUD also reported lower psychological well-being, social satisfaction, and self-efficacy, suggesting impaired positive emotional functioning as well.

This dual vulnerability is important considering that emotional health reflects not only the absence of distress but also the presence of positive affect, reward responsiveness, and psychological fulfillment (Fredrickson, 2000; Fredrickson and Losada, 2005; Park et al., 2023).
text.formatted: This dual vulnerability is important considering that emotional health reflects not only the absence of distress but also the presence of positive affect, reward responsiveness, and psychological fulfillment <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Fredrickson, 2000;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Fredrickson and Losada, 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Park et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Although our data cannot resolve whether these associations are causal in nature, these differences may reflect enduring changes in the neural circuits implicated in emotion regulation associated with alcohol and cannabis use disorders (Estrada-Medina et al., 2026; Wilcox et al., 2016).
text.formatted: Although our data cannot resolve whether these associations are causal in nature, these differences may reflect enduring changes in the neural circuits implicated in emotion regulation associated with alcohol and cannabis use disorders <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Estrada-Medina et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Wilcox et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, diminished positive emotions may be an important and enduring vulnerability among adults with a lifetime history of comorbid AUD and CUD, which has potential implications for both poorer physical health (Pressman et al., 2019) and, for those in remission, likelihood of returning to problematic use.
text.formatted: Thus, diminished positive emotions may be an important and enduring vulnerability among adults with a lifetime history of comorbid AUD and CUD, which has potential implications for both poorer physical health <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Pressman et al., 2019)</ref> and, for those in remission, likelihood of returning to problematic use.

text.text: The significance of this mechanism has been illustrated for depression and anxiety, where diminished positive affect and impaired reward processing have been linked to greater chronicity, functional impairment, and poorer treatment outcomes (Meuret et al., 2026).

text.text: Whether this also holds true for substance use disorder treatment remains unknown given the limited attention to positive affect in this context (Swan et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Whether this also holds true for substance use disorder treatment remains unknown given the limited attention to positive affect in this context <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Swan et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Although the comorbid group showed the most widespread difficulties, the AUD+/CUDgroup also differed in specific ways from people with neither disorder.
Individuals with AUD without CUD reported significantly greater negative affect, lower social satisfaction, and lower psychological well-being than the AUD-/CUD-group.

This pattern aligns with prior work linking AUD to heightened negative emotionality and to strained interpersonal relationships and reduced social support (Stellern et al., 2023), suggesting that AUD in the absence of CUD is associated with challenges in these specific domains, even if narrower than those seen in the comorbid group.
text.formatted: This pattern aligns with prior work linking AUD to heightened negative emotionality and to strained interpersonal relationships and reduced social support <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Stellern et al., 2023)</ref>, suggesting that AUD in the absence of CUD is associated with challenges in these specific domains, even if narrower than those seen in the comorbid group.

text.text: In contrast, and contrary to our hypotheses, individuals with CUD without AUD did not differ from those with neither disorder on any emotional well-being outcome after covariate adjustment.
This null finding should be interpreted cautiously, as the AUD-/CUD+ group was the smallest diagnostic group (n=84), limiting statistical power to detect differences.
Several factors may contribute to the more pronounced difficulties observed in the comorbid group.

Comorbid AUD and CUD may reflect greater overall disorder severity, cumulative emotional burden (i.e., the compounded emotional strain of experiencing two disorders rather than one) (Briere et al., 2011; Hetelekides et al., 2025), more chronic maladaptive coping patterns (Adan et al., 2017), or other common psychiatric comorbidities such as major depression (McHugh and Weiss, 2019).

text.text: The overall pattern of findings was robust to adjustment for lifetime MDD.
The one exception was self-efficacy, where differences between the comorbid group and the AUD-/CUD-and AUD+/CUD-groups were attenuated.
In other words, the reduced confidence in one's ability to manage challenges observed in the comorbid group may reflect people's history of major depression as much as substance use comorbidity.

text.text: A key implication of the present findings is that a lifetime history of comorbid AUD and CUD is associated with poorer emotional well-being that goes above and beyond both recent substance use and lifetime major depression.

This points to the long-reaching challenges to emotional health experienced by people with comorbid AUD and CUD, and suggests that efforts to improve outcomes for those with comorbid CUD and AUD will likely benefit from broader, longer-term psychosocial support that directly addresses positive as well as negative emotional functioning (Adan et al., 2017; Sinha, 2024; Stellern et al., 2023).

text.text: Second, because diagnostic groups were defined using lifetime measures, we could not determine whether individuals AUD and CUD were active concurrently.
An individual who met criteria for CUD earlier in life, remitted, and later developed AUD would be classified as comorbid despite never having both disorders active at the same time.
As such, the comorbid group likely includes heterogeneous patterns of temporal co-occurrence.

Our approach to defining the diagnostic groups was informed by prior evidence that lifetime comorbidity is clinically meaningful, as a history of either disorder, even in remission, may alter the course, treatment, or prognosis of the other (Metrik et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Our approach to defining the diagnostic groups was informed by prior evidence that lifetime comorbidity is clinically meaningful, as a history of either disorder, even in remission, may alter the course, treatment, or prognosis of the other <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Metrik et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Although we adjusted for past-year substance use, future research aimed at understanding whether associations differ across stages and co-occurrence of disorder may offer a more nuanced picture.
Incorporating remission status into the present analyses was considered but was complicated by statistical constraints.

For example, stratifying each diagnostic group by remission status would have added five additional levels to the models, substantially increasing the number of comparisons while reducing the resulting subgroup sizes, making them too small to support stable or interpretable estimates.

Relatedly, because remission is conditional on having a diagnosis, there was no straightforward way to directly model remission as a separate covariate because unaffected individuals would be, by definition, set to missing.
This would have the consequence of unaffected individuals being excluded from the analysis due to missingness on this covariate, obscuring the differences of interest.
Attention to remission remains an important direction for future work in samples that are better powered to explore these potential differences.
Third, the analyses were correlational in nature, and therefore, causal conclusions regarding the relationship between AUD, CUD, and emotional well-being cannot be drawn.
Fourth, although models adjusted for several relevant covariates, other potentially important factors influencing emotional well-being not measured here may contribute to the observed associations.

In conclusion, we found that individuals with a lifetime history of both AUD and CUD experienced poorer emotional well-being than those with a single disorder or no lifetime history of either, showing both reduced positive emotions and elevated negative emotions.
These associations remained significant even after accounting for past-year substance use and history of major depression.

As a set, these findings suggest that people with comorbid substance use disorders may experience broad and enduring emotional difficulties and may benefit from psychosocial supports to address these challenges.

text.text: Clinical guidance is complicated by the increasing use of cannabis for medical reasons, which may point to other comorbid physical or mental health conditions that may also impact wellbeing, such as chronic pain.

Furthermore, while aftercare is recommended, adherence to these recommendations often involves addressing related issues such as availability, affordability, logistics (e.g., managing around work and caregiving responsibilities), and motivation.
Additional attention to treatment that addresses these complexities may help to improve outcomes for those with comorbid AUD and CUD.
Several limitations should be considered when interpreting the findings.
First, the COGA sample represents a high-risk, family-based cohort (Dick et al., 2023), which may limit the generalizability of the results to broader population samples.
